opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the places where I'm a little more skeptical than a lot of the interpretability community, and I want to be careful about how I say it, because I think sparse autoencoders are genuinely interesting and I'm glad people are working on them.

The thing that adversarial examples taught us, going back now more than a decade, is that the features a model actually uses to make decisions are not necessarily the features we'd like it to use. You can take an image of a panda, change every pixel by an amount you literally cannot see, and the model is now extremely confident it's a gibbon. Whatever the model is responding to there, it's not "panda-ness" in any sense a human would recognize. And there's a well-known line of work arguing that these perturbations aren't bugs at all; they're exploiting features that are genuinely predictive on the training distribution but just aren't meaningful to us.

So when I look at a sparse autoencoder and it says, "here's feature 31,415, it fires on the Golden Gate Bridge," my first question is: what fraction of the model's behavior does that explanation actually account for? Because SAEs have reconstruction error. There's a residual they don't capture. And my worry, as an attacker, is that the residual is exactly where the interesting stuff lives. If I wanted to make a model do something bad, I'd go looking in precisely the directions the dictionary doesn't explain well.

I'd also say that "interpretable" is doing a lot of work in these papers. Usually what it means is that we looked at the top-activating examples and a human, or another language model, said "oh, these all look like they're about X." That's a pretty weak test. It tells you about the extremes of the distribution, not about what the feature does in the middle, and it tells you nothing about what happens when an adversary is actively trying to push activations into weird regions. Under attack, you could imagine driving the "Golden Gate Bridge" feature up with an input that has nothing to do with bridges at all. The label stays the same; the meaning has quietly evaporated.

So how do I reconcile them? I think they're answering different questions. SAEs are giving us a pretty good description of what the model is doing on typical inputs. Adversarial examples are telling us what the model is capable of doing on worst-case inputs. Both are true at the same time. Where I get nervous is when people take the first kind of result and use it to make claims of the second kind, like, "we've found the deception feature, so we can monitor for it and we're safe." That's a security claim, and security claims have to survive an adaptive adversary. I'd love to see interpretability papers include an attack section, where you explicitly try to make the model do the bad thing without lighting up the feature you're monitoring. If the method survives that, great, I'll be very excited. Historically, almost every defense that hasn't been evaluated that way has fallen over pretty quickly once someone tried.

r001.rationale: The response says SAEs describe behavior on typical inputs while adversarial examples reveal capabilities on worst-case inputs, and that both can be true at once.

r002.rationale: It says adversarial attacks can exploit features that are predictive on the training distribution but not meaningful to humans, then suggests such features may live in the residual SAEs do not explain.

r003.rationale: The response describes adversarial perturbations causing a panda image to be classified as a gibbon, but does not explain that an attacker strongly activates a highly weighted non-robust feature to override other predictive cues.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I don't fully reconcile them, and I think that's actually the interesting part.

Let me start with what I think the adversarial examples work has been telling us for about a decade now. When you take an image classifier and you perturb the pixels by an amount that's imperceptible to a human, and the model flips from "panda" to "gibbon," the natural first reaction is "the model is broken, it's latched onto some bug." And then there was this line of work, the "adversarial examples are features, not bugs" paper, that said, no, actually, those perturbations correspond to real statistical regularities in the training distribution. The model is picking up on things that genuinely predict the label. They just happen to be things that humans don't see and don't care about.

And I think that's important context for the sparse autoencoder work, because what an SAE is doing is taking the activations of a model and trying to decompose them into some overcomplete basis where each direction is hopefully monosemantic. And then a human looks at the top-activating examples and says, "ah, this is the Golden Gate Bridge feature" or "this is the feature for code that has a bug in it." And a lot of those are really compelling. I don't want to be dismissive of that work, I think it's some of the best interpretability work that's been done.

But here's where I get nervous. The step where a human labels the feature is doing a lot of work. The feature is a direction in activation space. The human's story about what it means is a compression of that direction into a sentence. And the adversarial examples literature is essentially a ten-year-long demonstration that the directions models actually use are frequently not the directions humans would write a sentence about. So when I see a dictionary of ten million features and most of them have a nice label, my prior is that for some fraction of those, the label captures maybe the majority of the variance of that feature, but the tail of it, the part that activates on inputs that don't look like the top examples, is exactly the part an attacker would use.

And in fact, we've started to see this empirically. You can take an SAE, you can find a feature that's supposedly "about" one thing, and then you can construct inputs that activate it strongly that have nothing to do with the human description. That's just an adversarial example against the explanation rather than against the classifier. It's the same phenomenon one level up.

So I think the way I'd reconcile them is: sparse autoencoders are giving you an approximate, human-readable summary of a thing that is not fundamentally human-readable. That summary is useful. It's useful the same way a summary of a long document is useful. It's going to be right most of the time on the distribution the summary was written from. But you should not expect it to hold up under optimization pressure, because nothing holds up under optimization pressure unless it was specifically built to. And the moment you want to use interpretability for something adversarial, like, "I want to guarantee this model won't do X," you're now in a regime where the gap between the feature and its explanation matters a lot, and that's the gap adversarial examples live in.

I'd also say, as someone who spends most of my time breaking things, the interesting question is not "are SAE explanations correct" in some binary sense. It's "how much does it cost to make them wrong." If it takes a lot of optimization to find an input where the explanation fails, that's a meaningfully better situation than if it takes a little. And I think that's a quantity people should actually be measuring rather than just showing the top-k activating examples and calling it done.

r001.rationale: The response presents SAE descriptions as useful human-readable summaries while arguing that adversarial attacks can exploit model directions those descriptions miss, so the two can coexist.

r002.rationale: It says adversarially useful directions can capture real statistical regularities that predict labels, while SAE explanations may miss the directions' less interpretable parts.

r003.rationale: It mentions inputs that strongly activate a feature and adversarial examples that flip predictions, but does not explain that an attacker overrides other predictive cues through a highly weighted non-robust feature.

astra-6.text:
I think the reconciliation is that an explanation can be useful without being complete. A sparse autoencoder gives you a way to decompose a model’s activations into features, and sometimes you can look at a feature and say, “Oh, this seems to correspond to a particular concept.” But that’s a much weaker claim than saying we understand everything the model uses to make its decisions.

Even naming a feature is tricky. If the examples that activate it all have something in common, we give it that label. But we haven’t necessarily characterized what activates it on every possible input. An adversarial attack is very good at finding the places where that human description stops matching what the model actually computes.

And an attack doesn’t necessarily have to exploit some completely uninterpretable feature. It could exploit a combination of features we understand individually, or push an otherwise recognizable feature into a regime we haven’t studied.

So I would use adversarial attacks as a test of the explanations. If we think we understand a mechanism, can we predict what an intervention will do? Can we construct an input that breaks that prediction? When we can, that tells us something is missing. That doesn’t make sparse autoencoders useless. It gives us a way to distinguish an explanation that sounds plausible from one that actually lets us predict the model’s behavior.

r001.rationale: The response says an explanation can be useful without being complete and that attacks may exploit behavior outside the human description, including potentially uninterpretable features.

r002.rationale: It does not say that features sparse autoencoders cannot interpret are non-robust features useful for prediction.

r003.rationale: It does not describe strongly activating a highly weighted non-robust feature to override other predictive cues and cause a wrong prediction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the thing to keep in mind is that an explanation can be useful without being complete. With a sparse autoencoder, you might find a feature that activates on examples that all look related to us, and give it a nice human-readable label. But that doesn’t establish that the label fully describes what the feature computes, or that we’ve captured everything the model is using.

An adversarial attack asks a different question: can I find an input where the model behaves in a way that violates my expectations? And the attack can search precisely for cases that our explanation doesn’t cover. A feature might look very interpretable on ordinary inputs and behave quite differently on inputs optimized to activate it.

So I don’t see these as contradictory. I see adversarial attacks as a way to test how much an interpretability result actually tells us. If you think you’ve identified the mechanism behind some behavior, can you use that understanding to predict what happens under an attack? Can you intervene on the feature and reliably change the behavior? That’s a stronger claim than having examples that fit a compelling description.

The distinction I’d make is between finding something we can understand in a model and understanding the model well enough that it can’t surprise us. Sparse autoencoders can help with the first. The second is a much higher bar.

r001.rationale: The response says sparse autoencoders can reveal interpretable features while adversarial attacks expose behavior those explanations do not cover, and explicitly says the two are not contradictory.

r002.rationale: It says a feature may behave differently on inputs optimized to activate it, but does not characterize uninterpretable features as non-robust features useful for prediction.

r003.rationale: It does not describe an attacker strongly activating a highly weighted non-robust feature to override other predictive cues and cause a wrong prediction.
